strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important gap: efficient, numerically tight privacy loss accounting for random allocation (used in DP-SGD variants such as balls-and-bins/PREAMBLE), improving substantially over prior RDP/hockey-stick approximations from Feldman & Shenfeld (2025) and Dong et al. (2025), which incur up to ~20-60% looseness in epsilon.

Clean and non-trivial theoretical contribution: the notion of PLD realization and the characterization of the random-allocation PLD as a (t-wise) convolution of exponentiated PLDs (exp-PLDs) and their PLD duals is an elegant reduction that enables efficient, provably tight numerical computation (Theorem 4.4, 4.6).

Rigorous complexity analysis (O(log^3(t) log(t/beta)/alpha^2)) with matching stochastic-domination-based tightness guarantees (alpha, beta), including both upper and lower bounds, which is unusual rigor for this line of empirical PLD-accounting work.

Strong empirical validation: numerical bounds nearly match Monte Carlo simulation results and known lower bounds (Fig. 1, 2, 6), and the method is shown practical (seconds to tens of seconds) across realistic parameter regimes (Fig. 3).

Broader methodological contribution beyond random allocation: shows how to perform Poisson subsampling directly on PLD realizations (Theorem 3.3), generalizing accurate accounting beyond composition to any dominated algorithm, not just Gaussian/Laplace mechanisms as in current libraries.

Demonstrates real practical impact by improving privacy accounting for the PREAMBLE communication-efficient DP-SGD algorithm (Asi et al., 2025), showing meaningfully tighter noise-vs-privacy tradeoffs than RDP-based accounting used in the original work (Fig. 5).

Thorough treatment of implementation details (full pseudocode in Appendix C), numerical stability considerations, and comparison between FFT-based and direct multiplicative convolution approaches, aiding reproducibility; code is released.
weaknesses: No new utility/accuracy experiments beyond a single toy mean-estimation replication (Fig. 4); the paper explicitly defers to prior work for utility claims, which is reasonable given the privacy-accounting focus but means the paper's practical value proposition ("random allocation now provably beats Poisson for DP-SGD utility") rests partly on combining this paper's bounds with separate, previously published utility results rather than a unified empirical demonstration.

The paper is extremely dense with heavy notation, multiple domination/duality notions (hockey-stick domination, stochastic domination, PLD duals, exp-PLD transforms), and deferred proofs, which may limit accessibility and reproducibility for readers not already steeped in the PLD-accounting literature; the main text is largely a technical overview with most substance in the appendix.

The FFT-based convolution alternative is presented without formal tightness/error guarantees (only empirical validity), leaving a gap between the theoretically-justified direct multiplicative method and the practically-relevant FFT alternative discussed in Section 5.

The reduction from general k-out-of-t to k=1 composition (Lemma 2.8, from prior work) is acknowledged as lossy, particularly when t/k is small (Fig. 11 shows visible gaps for large k relative to t), so the paper's tightness claims are strongest primarily in the k=1 regime.

Numerical stability limitations are noted only qualitatively (float64 breaks down below ~1e-15, requiring float128 with added cost) without a rigorous treatment of how this interacts with the paper's own tightness guarantees in extreme small-delta, high-composition regimes (e.g., the PREAMBLE experiment mentions "heavy computation load" and needing 1e6 bins, suggesting practical scalability concerns are non-trivial in the most demanding settings).

strengths: Addresses a practically important gap: existing analyses of k-out-of-t random allocation (Feldman & Shenfeld 2025; Dong et al. 2025) are either loose or incompatible with efficient PLD-based accounting pipelines used in practice (Opacus, dp_accounting, PRV accountant).

The core technical idea -- representing the PLD of random allocation as a (log of a) convolution of exponentiated PLDs (exp-PLDs) and their duals -- is a clean and non-obvious reduction (Theorem 4.4) that enables efficient numerical computation rather than relying on Monte Carlo estimation or loose analytic bounds.

The paper provides formal validity, tightness (α,β), and runtime guarantees (Theorem 4.6), with an explicit, fully specified algorithm (Appendix C) including handling of numerical stability concerns, which aids reproducibility.

The notion of 'PLD realization' is a nice unifying abstraction that lets the same machinery handle composition, Poisson subsampling, and random allocation on a common representation, and is likely of independent interest to the DP accounting community.

Numerical results are fairly convincing: the computed bounds nearly match Monte Carlo estimates and lower bounds in regimes where MC is reliable, and are substantially tighter than prior analytic (RDP/ (ε,δ)) bounds, including in a realistic nested-sampling application (PREAMBLE/DP-SGD).
Runtime experiments support the claimed polylog(t) · 1/α² scaling, and the method is shown to be practical (seconds on a laptop) for parameter ranges relevant to DP-SGD.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely an efficient numerical procedure built on top of reductions and dominating-pair constructions established in prior work (Feldman & Shenfeld 2025; Chua et al. 2024a; Dong et al. 2025); the paper's novelty is concentrated in the discretization/convolution scheme rather than in new structural insight about random allocation itself.

The reduction from general k to k=1 (Lemma 2.8, reused from prior work) is acknowledged to be lossy, and Figure 11 confirms the resulting k>1 bounds can be visibly suboptimal when t mod k is non-negligible -- so the 'near-tightness' claim is really only well-supported for k=1.

No direct empirical validation of the headline claim that 'random allocation is at least as good as Poisson for DP-SGD utility' on real training tasks; the utility side is entirely borrowed from other papers' experiments and only combined post-hoc with this paper's privacy numbers, rather than demonstrated end-to-end.

The method's practicality in very-high-precision regimes (e.g., the PREAMBLE experiment needing 10^6 bins per direction) suggests the quadratic-in-1/α, IQR-dependent cost could become a real bottleneck for small δ or many composition rounds, and the paper's own numerical-stability discussion (float128, Kahan summation) signals this is a nontrivial engineering burden, not just a theoretical footnote.

FFT-based convolution, the standard tool in the PLD literature, is shown not to work well here without explicit tightness guarantees, and the proposed alternative (direct multiplicative convolution) is itself only heuristically combined with FFT for best results (Appendix D), leaving open questions about a principled unified approach.

Presentation is dense and backloads most substantive derivations, algorithms, and proofs to the appendix, leaving the main text to largely narrate results; this limits the self-containedness and accessibility of the submission for readers who cannot engage with ~30 pages of appendix material.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: tight, efficient privacy accounting for the random allocation (balls-and-bins / k-out-of-t) sampling scheme that is increasingly used in DP-SGD and communication-efficient private aggregation, where prior analyses (Feldman & Shenfeld 2025; Dong et al. 2025) were known to be loose or RDP/(ε,δ)-specific.

Solid theoretical contribution: the notion of 'PLD realization' and the associated domination-preserving transformations (Theorem 3.3 for subsampling, Theorem 4.4 for random allocation) is a clean and general abstraction that extends standard PLD accounting beyond composition to subsampling and random allocation, with careful formal treatment of both add/remove directions and of approximation tightness via (α,β)-stochastic domination.
Rigorous complexity analysis (Theorem 4.6) with explicit polylog(t)/α^2 runtime, and the algorithm is empirically shown to be practical (seconds to tens of seconds) even for large t.

Strong empirical validation: the proposed upper bounds are nearly indistinguishable from matching lower bounds and from Monte Carlo estimates in reliable regimes, and are substantially tighter than prior analytic bounds (FS25, DCO25) across a range of t, σ, and k, including k>1.

Demonstrated utility of the method on a realistic downstream application (DP-SGD with PREAMBLE for low-communication aggregation), showing meaningful noise-level/accuracy improvements over RDP-based accounting in a nontrivial composition setting.

Honest and detailed discussion of implementation trade-offs (FFT vs. direct multiplicative convolution, numerical stability issues, combination of bounds via Claim B.3), with full algorithmic pseudocode and proofs in the appendix, and an implementation reference, supporting reproducibility.

Both upper and lower bound algorithms are provided, which is useful for empirically certifying tightness without relying solely on Monte Carlo methods that are hard to scale to small δ or many compositions.
weaknesses: No new empirical utility (accuracy) evaluation of training with random allocation is provided; the paper relies entirely on prior work's utility results and a repeated toy experiment, so the practical end-to-end benefit of tighter privacy accounting for real DP-SGD training workloads is not directly demonstrated.

The reduction from general k-out-of-t to k-fold composition of 1-out-of-⌊t/k⌋ (Lemma 2.8) is acknowledged to be lossy when t/k is small or t mod k is non-negligible (Figure 11), and the paper does not propose a tighter direct treatment of general k, leaving a gap for some parameter regimes.

The computational cost can become substantial in demanding settings (e.g., the PREAMBLE experiment needed 10^6 bins per direction due to heavy composition), suggesting that for very small δ combined with long composition chains the method may still face practical scalability limits, although the authors are transparent about this.

The comparison between FFT-based and direct multiplicative convolution approaches is somewhat ad hoc (no principled automatic method to choose or combine them beyond manually taking the better of the two bounds), which slightly undercuts the claim of a fully turnkey accounting solution.

Presentation is dense and highly technical, with many definitions, lemmas, and algorithmic details split across the main text and a lengthy appendix; a reader unfamiliar with the PLD/dominating-pair formalism may find it difficult to follow without closely cross-referencing prior work (Zhu et al. 2022; Gopi et al. 2021; Feldman & Shenfeld 2025).
